channel.title: OT/ICS Threat Intel - Rail
channel.description: Curated OT/ICS advisories, incidents and threat intelligence. Editorial by Mike Holcomb in partnership with UtilSec.

item.title: [Critical] Renfe says the stolen passenger data came from previously compromised Adif servers, and Adif says no rail-operations system was touched — the 500 GB and AI-tooling accounts are still unconfirmed
item.category: Top Story
item.description: Adif, Spain’s state railway infrastructure manager, detected unusual activity in its systems late on Thursday 24 September, took its own and Adif Alta Velocidad’s websites offline as a precaution, and restored them on Saturday 26 September. On Friday 25 September Renfe, the state train operator, said passenger data had been obtained and that it originated on Adif servers that had been compromised earlier; it described the data as limited, mainly names and email addresses, with no impact on banking or financial information, and it has not said how many passengers are affected. Adif’s own statement answers the operational question: no application or system related to railway operations was affected, and trains ran normally. Two widely repeated details remain unconfirmed. A figure of about 500 GB of stolen data and an account of AI tools being used to probe for weaknesses were first aired in Spanish media on 25 September, and neither Renfe nor Adif has confirmed either. The security firm Shieldworkz added an analysis on 30 September, reported by Industrial Cyber: weeks of reconnaissance and brute-force attempts against Adif’s external web infrastructure from late August, a pivot through legacy interconnections into Renfe IT, the 500 GB figure, and what it labels a strongly supported but unconfirmed claim of “automated AI-driven exploitation agents”. Shieldworkz gives an Iranian-actor hypothesis only low confidence, and no actor, ransomware group or leak-site claim has been identified; its volume, tooling and attribution points are one firm’s analysis, not official findings. This is an IT and customer-data incident, not an OT one, and it does not move the threat level into the incident band. It stays the lead because it is still the only confirmed intrusion at a national rail operator in the lookback window, and because of the route: data held by the train operator was reached through the infrastructure manager’s servers, which its systems were connected to by design. Most railways have the same kind of link — between infrastructure manager and train operator, host railroad and tenant, or transit authority and contracted operator — and it is rarely scoped as an attack path. - Renfe and Adif statements as reported by Europa Press (via Alicante Plaza) and AFP (via The Local); Shieldworkz analysis as reported by Industrial Cyber; the 500 GB, AI-tooling and attribution points are unconfirmed; the partner-link framing is our editorial assessment - Adif detection 24 Sep 2026; Renfe statement 25 Sep 2026; Adif websites restored 26 Sep 2026; Shieldworkz analysis 30 Sep 2026

item.title: [High] A suspected China-linked group stole SCADA and HMI source code from an automation vendor — the repositories were self-hosted, reachable and running an unpatched Gitea
item.category: Incident — State-linked theft of industrial engineering material
item.description: Acronis threat intelligence published findings on 13 September on an actor it calls Red Heron, which has been exploiting CVE-2026-60004, a critical remote code execution flaw in self-hosted Gitea, since 29 July 2026. The group scanned 1,386 internet-facing Gitea instances across seven countries and confirmed compromises at 11 organisations in five countries, by Acronis’s count (some secondary reports give higher figures). Two victims matter here. A Taiwanese industrial-automation company lost repositories covering SCADA and HMI tooling, IoT platform integrations and network-sniffer products. A Canadian renewable-energy firm lost infrastructure maps, configuration secrets, SSH host keys and internal tokens. The toolset includes the JITTERLY Linux implant, a new self-restoring LD_PRELOAD rootkit Acronis calls SIXZUT, and the Adaptix C2 framework. Attribution to a Chinese-speaking group is moderate confidence, resting on language artefacts and tradecraft; the compromises themselves are confirmed. No rail organisation is among the named victims, but the exposure class is one transit owns outright: signalling, SCADA and passenger-information work is contracted out, and the contractor’s repository server holds the project files, controller logic and credentials for your estate. - Acronis threat intelligence — reported by Industrial Cyber and The Hacker News - Acronis report 13 Sep 2026; exploitation traced back to 29 Jul 2026; KEV-listed 25 Aug 2026

item.title: [Medium] Coordinated track sabotage stopped Dutch trains for a morning — physical, not cyber, and the fail-safe did exactly what it is designed to do
item.category: Incident — Physical sabotage of signalling infrastructure, not cyber
item.description: On the morning of Tuesday 15 September, the day of the Dutch state opening of parliament, ProRail found steel pipes up to two metres long fixed to the rails at somewhere between twenty and thirty locations, including the Amersfoort–Zwolle, Zwolle–Leeuwarden, Utrecht–Arnhem, Arnhem–Zutphen, Amersfoort–Deventer and Gouda–Oudewater lines. A pipe bridging the two rails shorts the track circuit, so the occupancy detection reports a train that is not there and the protecting signals hold at red. The first was found at about 05:30; one train struck a pipe near Steenwijk without injury; services north of Utrecht were worst affected, with knock-on disruption to German connections, and most of the network was restored by the afternoon. ProRail said the material had been placed intentionally; the AIVD intelligence service is working with police; no suspect has been named and a farmers’ protest group publicly denied involvement. This was physical sabotage with no reported cyber component, and it does not change the cyber threat level on this page. It is here because it was the only rail incident in the week it happened and because the mechanism is instructive: an attacker who understood signalling chose to trigger the safety case rather than defeat it, and the result was delay rather than danger. That is the outcome a track circuit or axle counter is engineered to produce, and it is the same outcome a defender should expect from a well-designed vital system under most cyber conditions — a fail-safe stop, with the operational cost carried in disruption. - DutchNews and NBC News reporting of ProRail and Dutch government statements; classification as physical sabotage is per those statements, and the fail-safe framing is our editorial assessment - Event 15 Sep 2026; reported 15 Sep 2026; no cyber component reported as of 24 Sep 2026

item.title: [High] Mandiant says ShinyHunters is back exploiting Oracle PeopleSoft by encoding one letter past WAF rules — transportation is among the sectors with compromised systems
item.category: Threat Intelligence & Research — Mass exploitation of an enterprise application, transportation among sectors hit
item.description: Google Threat Intelligence and Mandiant reported on 25 September a renewed mass-exploitation campaign by UNC6240, the group known as ShinyHunters, against CVE-2026-35273, an unauthenticated remote code execution flaw in the PeopleSoft Environment Management Hub (the /PSEMHUB/ path), rated CVSS v3.1 9.8. The flaw was first exploited as a zero-day against academic institutions in late May and early June, and Oracle has had a fix out since June. The new wave requests /%50SEMHUB/ instead: WAF rules that match the literal path miss it, and WebLogic decodes and routes the request anyway, reaching, in Mandiant’s words, “systems whose operators may have believed their WAF rules had mitigated the exposure”. Mandiant counts “dozens of systems” compromised globally across higher education, technology and IT services, healthcare, agriculture, transportation and government, names no victims, and says it has notified more than 100 organisations whose addresses matched vulnerable endpoints. The tooling includes JSP web shells, Neo-reGeorg tunnels, a SIDEEYE backdoor delivered in a trojanised Light Alloy media-player installer, and MeshAgent. CISA has listed CVE-2026-35273 in the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue since 12 June 2026 and marks it as known to be used in ransomware campaigns. The rail relevance is our editorial assessment: many transit authorities and railroads run PeopleSoft for HR, payroll and finance, and a web shell on that tier puts employee records and whatever directory and database credentials the application holds within an attacker’s reach. It is an IT-side risk, not an OT one. - Google Threat Intelligence / Mandiant report; corroborated by BleepingComputer and The Hacker News; CVSS v3.1 score per the published CVE record and KEV status per the CISA catalogue; rail relevance is our editorial assessment - Mandiant report 25 Sep 2026; KEV-listed 12 Jun 2026

item.title: [Low] A security researcher found a rail operator’s production database exposed with live administrator sessions — routes, schedules and announcements were one step away
item.category: Threat Intelligence & Research — Researcher-found exposure at an unnamed rail operator, IT/web, not exploited
item.description: Wiz published results of its “Scan for Good” programme on 24 September: an AI-assisted scan of public-facing systems at critical-infrastructure organisations, run with a supporting statement from CISA’s acting director. One finding concerns a public rail operator, which Wiz does not name or place in a country. In Wiz’s words, “a leaked production database exposed active administrator sessions, enabling control of routes, schedules, service announcements, and administrator accounts.” Wiz says it worked with the operator to secure the system before public transportation could be disrupted. Nothing in the report indicates that an attacker found or used the exposure, and no train-control, signalling or other OT system is described — this is the web and back-office layer. It is on this page because of what that layer controls. Passenger-information, scheduling and service-announcement platforms are rarely inside the TSA critical-cyber-system boundary, yet a hijacked administrator session there can publish false departures, cancel services on screen or push misleading announcements across stations — a disruption passengers experience as the railway itself failing. - Wiz research blog “Scan for Good” (verified 25 Sep 2026); also reported by Cybersecurity Dive; rail relevance is our editorial assessment - Published 24 Sep 2026

item.title: [Medium] Recorded Future expects Russia’s hybrid pressure on Europe to escalate over two years — logistics firms are flagged as high-risk, though no rail incident is cited
item.category: Threat Intelligence & Research — Analytic assessment of Russia-linked hybrid activity in Europe; no rail incident cited
item.description: Recorded Future’s Insikt Group published an assessment on 24 September that Russia has escalated what Insikt calls “New Generation Warfare” (NGW) tactics in Europe since February 2022. It describes current activity as “largely opportunistic” rather than a coordinated campaign, but judges Russia “likely to escalate NGW tactics over the next two years, potentially culminating in a full-scale NGW campaign.” The incidents it cites include an explosive maritime drone intercepted near Romania’s Neptun Deep offshore gas field on 20 August, a sabotage plot using military-grade explosives against cargo infrastructure at Germany’s Leipzig/Halle Airport in August, DDoS and access operations against the Norwegian public sector on 30 August, and Russian drones in Estonian airspace on 1 September. Its analyst adds that “outside of traditional critical infrastructure, logistics and dual-use firms are at high risk.” Recommendations include contractor and insider vetting, perimeter detection and counter-drone measures, law-enforcement partnerships, alternative supply routes, coordination with national CERTs and phishing-resistant MFA. The attribution is Insikt’s analytic assessment, and no specific unit is named. Nothing in it concerns a railway, and nothing links it to the Dutch track sabotage elsewhere on this page. It is here as context for European operators, and the rail relevance is our editorial assessment: the pattern it describes pairs physical interference with cyber and information operations, which is exactly the combination a rail incident process has to tell apart quickly. - Recorded Future Insikt Group blog; reported by Dark Reading; rail relevance is our editorial assessment - Published 24 Sep 2026

item.title: [Info] FDD warns that NATO reinforcement across Europe runs through civilian ports and railways with uneven cyber rules — and that Chinese-linked firms operate terminals in about half the EU ports NATO relies on
item.category: Threat Intelligence & Research — Think-tank analysis of military-mobility corridors; no incident
item.description: The Foundation for Defense of Democracies published a report on 28 September by Jiwon Ma, a senior policy analyst at its Center on Cyber and Technology Innovation, titled Strengthening NATO Through Military Mobility and Critical Infrastructure Cybersecurity. As reported by Industrial Cyber, it finds that three port groups — COSCO Shipping, China Merchants Group and Hutchison Port Holdings — own or operate terminals in roughly half of the EU ports considered critical to NATO operations; that firms FDD describes as Chinese state-linked hold stakes in more than 30 European port terminals, including facilities designated to receive US forces; and that they operate at no fewer than 14 of the 29 European ports near NATO naval facilities. For rail, the report’s point is scale and dependency: it notes that moving a single light division can take up to 200 trains, and that rail, unlike military air transport, has no mechanism for pooling assets, so it recommends jointly procuring or designating a minimum pool of dual-use heavy-lift wagons. Its cyber finding is that governance split across NATO, the EU and national authorities leaves the civilian transport operators that alliance forces depend on without consistent security standards. Other recommendations include aligning investment with reinforcement plans, annual national military-mobility annexes, organising NATO cyber-defence work around critical-infrastructure operators, tighter EU investment screening on military corridors, measures against satellite interference, and treating cyber workforce shortages as a defence priority. This is policy analysis from a think tank, not an incident or a government finding, and it names no compromised operator. The rail relevance for European infrastructure managers and freight operators on reinforcement corridors is our editorial assessment: a defence role can arrive without a matching security requirement, and the terminal at the port end of a rail movement may be run by a party whose systems you exchange data with but do not control. - Foundation for Defense of Democracies report by Jiwon Ma, as reported by Industrial Cyber; “Chinese state-linked” is FDD’s characterisation; rail relevance is our editorial assessment - Report published 28 Sep 2026

item.title: [Medium] Microsoft profiles Storm-2570, a ransomware affiliate that switches between Qilin, DragonForce, Anubis and BERT while its tradecraft stays the same — transportation is on its victim list
item.category: Threat Intelligence & Research — Ransomware affiliate profile, transportation among victim sectors
item.description: Microsoft Threat Intelligence published a profile on 24 September of Storm-2570, a ransomware affiliate it has tracked since April 2025 that deploys Qilin, DragonForce, Anubis or BERT depending on the operation. Victims are in the United States, Canada, the United Kingdom, Spain, the Netherlands and Puerto Rico, across sectors including transportation, energy, critical manufacturing, chemicals, healthcare, education, government and financial services. Microsoft says the group’s initial access “remains unconfirmed”. What stays consistent is what happens next: legitimate remote-management tools (Atera, MeshAgent, ScreenConnect, Splashtop and NinjaRMM), lateral movement with PsExec, Impacket and NetExec, credential theft with Mimikatz, LaZagne and ntdsutil, and exfiltration with Rclone and s5cmd. Microsoft names no victims and no rail operator is identified. The rail relevance is our editorial assessment: the point of the profile is that the ransomware brand changes while the behaviour does not, so detection built on tooling and behaviour — unapproved remote-management agents, PsExec from unexpected hosts, bulk Rclone transfers — keeps working when the ransom note names a different gang. - Microsoft Security Blog (Microsoft Threat Intelligence); rail relevance is our editorial assessment - Published 24 Sep 2026

item.title: [Info] CISA publishes a cyber-decoys guide — detection you can add without touching a vital system
item.category: Threat Intelligence & Research — Federal detection guidance
item.description: CISA released “Using Cyber Decoys to Strengthen Detection and Response” on 17 September. It defines decoys as assets that appear to be legitimate systems, accounts or data but exist to distract adversaries, reveal their presence and support threat-intelligence collection, and it sets out three phases — preparation, execution and analysis — positioning the technique alongside Zero Trust rather than as a replacement for it. The reason this matters more in rail than in most sectors is what it does not require. Decoys, honeytokens and tripwire accounts are additive: a credential that should never be used, a fake engineering share, a dummy historian tag, a service account that exists only to be alerted on. None of that changes a signalling, interlocking or traction-power system, which is normally the reason detection work stalls on a railway — the asset owner will not accept a change to a vital system for a monitoring benefit. This is guidance, not a threat item: no vulnerability, no incident and no product is involved. - CISA guide “Using Cyber Decoys to Strengthen Detection and Response” — corroborated by SecurityWeek and Industrial Cyber - Published 17 Sep 2026

item.title: [Medium] Two August counts, one direction: Comparitech logged a record 997 ransomware attacks and NCC Group 1,073, with industrial victims the largest share — and a newer group, Aurora, lists transportation among its targets
item.category: Threat Intelligence & Research — Sector statistics
item.description: Comparitech data reported on 14 September recorded 997 ransomware attacks worldwide in August 2026 — about 32 a day, 23 percent more than July’s 809 and above the previous monthly record of 988 — with utility, healthcare and business-services attacks singled out as the categories behind the rise. NCC Group’s August review, reported by Industrial Cyber on 28 September, counts 1,073 attacks, up 12 percent from 960 in July, with the industrial sector the largest target at 329 attacks (31 percent), North America at 473 (44 percent) and Europe at 276 (26 percent); Qilin led with 164, overtaking The Gentlemen. NCC also profiles Aurora, a ransomware-as-a-service group active since late April 2026 whose targets include manufacturing, legal, research and development, and transportation: it gets in through VPN exploitation and credential harvesting, then encrypts hypervisors, taking every hosted virtual machine down at once. Both counts rest on leak-site claims and disclosure practice, which is why the totals differ; claimed victims are not confirmed victims, and neither tracker names a rail operator. For rail and transit the exposure is rarely the signalling system itself — it is dispatch support, crew management, maintenance planning, fare collection and passenger information, much of which now runs as virtual machines on a small number of hypervisors. - Comparitech monthly ransomware tracking and NCC Group’s August 2026 review, both via Industrial Cyber; counts are leak-site based - Data for August 2026; reporting 14 Sep 2026 and 28 Sep 2026

item.title: [Info] Cyber-informed engineering argues the useful question is not how to keep attackers out, but which consequences you can design away
item.category: Threat Intelligence & Research — Analysis, engineering practice
item.description: An analysis published 15 September sets out the case for cyber-informed engineering in critical infrastructure: that industrial systems operate under a constraint IT does not share, because a compromised network does not automatically have to become a catastrophic physical event. The argument is to move the security question upstream into design — identifying the physical consequences that actually matter, then engineering them out with controls that do not depend on the digital system remaining trustworthy. Rail has practised this for a century without calling it cybersecurity: interlocking, fail-safe signalling and vital logic exist precisely so that a failure upstream cannot produce an unsafe movement. The current argument is that those principles should be applied deliberately to digital systems rather than assumed to still hold. This is practitioner analysis rather than incident reporting; it names no victim and describes no attack, but it is the most useful lens available for operators whose detection budget will never match their consequence exposure. - Industrial Cyber feature analysis on cyber-informed engineering - Published 15 Sep 2026

item.title: [High] Google’s threat intelligence group documents a credential campaign run end to end by autonomous agents in under six hours — and exploited vulnerabilities now arriving at about 18 a month
item.category: Threat Intel — Autonomous intrusion tooling and AI-era exploitation trends
item.description: Google’s Threat Intelligence Group reported on 8 September that a financially motivated group completed a large-scale credential-harvesting campaign in less than six hours using an autonomous multi-agent framework, with the agents rather than human operators carrying it through. GTIG separately observed actors stealing AI API credentials and running unauthorised workloads inside victims’ own cloud tenants across healthcare, government and media, and its guidance is to assume every actor is now using AI to some degree. On 30 September GTIG followed with data on vulnerability discovery and exploitation: monthly disclosures roughly doubled from 5,045 in January 2026 to 10,477 in July and reached 10,740 in August, while exploited vulnerabilities averaged 18 a month from January to August against 10.5 a month in 2025 — 141 distinct exploited flaws in eight months, against 127 in all of 2025. Edge and security appliances made up 14 percent of the exploited flaws, and more than 65 percent of those carried GTIG’s high or critical risk ratings; half of AI-discovered vulnerabilities were remote code execution, against 26 percent across the wider CVE ecosystem. GTIG does not discuss OT, industrial control systems or rail; that connection is ours. The rail consequence is arithmetic, not novelty. Credential phishing against dispatchers, crew callers, maintenance planners and contractor accounts is the standard opening move, and a campaign that completes inside six hours finishes well before a Monday-morning review — and comfortably inside the overnight window when the operations control centre is staffed but the security team is not. More exploited edge flaws each month also means the remote-access gear on this page’s advisory list will keep arriving faster than a slow patch cycle can absorb. - Google Threat Intelligence Group reporting of 8 Sep 2026, via The Hacker News; GTIG blog on vulnerability discovery and exploitation trends in the AI era; rail relevance is our editorial assessment - Published 8 Sep 2026 and 30 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] NetScaler’s zero-days are now vendor-confirmed and in KEV — two patched on 27 September, a third listed on 4 October with a 7 October deadline, and patching does not evict an intruder already inside
item.category: Critical Advisory — Remote-access gateway, three exploited zero-days, KEV-listed, suspected state-sponsored actors
item.description: Citrix confirmed on 27 September that two of the eight NetScaler ADC and NetScaler Gateway flaws fixed in bulletin CTX697096 had been exploited before patches existed, and CISA added both to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue the same day with a 30 September deadline. CVE-2026-88771 is improper input validation that allows unauthenticated command execution on any deployment, including the default configuration; CVE-2026-88772 is a memory overflow that can lead to code execution or denial of service where DTLS is enabled, which it is by default on VPN virtual servers. Citrix rates both CVSS v4 9.5. Fixed builds are 14.1-73.37 and 13.1-64.23 or later, so the 13.1 branch, past End of Maintenance since 15 September, did receive a fix. CISA said threat actors are exploiting the flaws globally and advised preserving forensic evidence before patching; the Dutch NCSC said exploitation had been identified at multiple Citrix customers worldwide. Mandiant attributes the activity to suspected state-sponsored actors and names no group. Victim counts come from different trackers and should not be merged: Mandiant says dozens of organisations across government, education, technology, finance, telecoms and professional services in North America and Europe; Arctic Wolf counts at least 78; the researcher Kevin Beaumont counted more than 100 by 29 September on his own tracking. Reported post-exploitation activity includes a PHP web shell, a Python tunneller, a rogue superuser account and theft of the appliance configuration archive, and Mandiant’s CTO warned that upgrading alone will not remove that access or the stolen credentials. Mass exploitation followed watchTowr’s technical write-up of 28 September. In the Netherlands the Interior Ministry took its Citrix environments offline and hospitals shut down some systems; those were precautionary shutdowns, not confirmed compromises. A third flaw, CVE-2026-88779, is a memory overflow that affects only appliances configured as a SAML service provider or identity provider (CVSS v4 8.7, fixed in 14.1-73.41 and 13.1-64.28 or later). Citrix confirmed targeted attacks that can cause denial of service, and CISA added it to KEV on 4 October with a 7 October deadline. watchTowr reproduced it as a crash-only bug and suspects it is used to knock appliances over to speed up exploitation of CVE-2026-88771; one researcher reported signs of code execution on a patched honeypot, but watchTowr and Citrix describe a crash, and Citrix says it has identified no impact on the integrity of customer data. No rail or transit victim has been named. The rail relevance is our editorial assessment: NetScaler Gateway is a common front door for supplier and remote-engineer access, and on many railways and transit agencies it is the path by which signalling, SCADA and fare-system contractors reach the OT DMZ. - Citrix bulletins CTX697096 and CTX697174 as summarised by Tenable; CISA alert and KEV records; Dutch NCSC via SecurityWeek and Help Net Security; Mandiant, Arctic Wolf and Kevin Beaumont via Cybersecurity Dive and Help Net Security; post-exploitation detail from LevelBlue and GTIG via The Hacker News; watchTowr via SecurityWeek; rail relevance is our editorial assessment - Patched and KEV-listed 27 Sep 2026; third flaw KEV-listed 4 Oct 2026, due 7 Oct 2026; watchTowr assessment 5 Oct 2026

item.title: [Critical] Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN Manager and Fortinet FortiMail join KEV as exploited zero-days — one configures the routers at every station and depot, the other screens mail into the corporate side
item.category: Critical Advisory — Actively exploited, KEV-listed, SD-WAN control plane and mail gateway
item.description: Cisco published an advisory on 30 September for CVE-2026-76504 in Catalyst SD-WAN Manager: improper handling of URI encoding lets a remote, unauthenticated attacker get past an authentication rule meant to protect an API endpoint and reach administrative-level access. Cisco scores it CVSS 9.8, offers no workaround, and says its PSIRT became aware of active exploitation in September; CISA added it to KEV the same day with a 3 October deadline, and Cisco revised the advisory on 2 October. Fixed releases are 20.9.10.1, 20.12.8.2, 20.15.6.1, 20.18.4.1, 26.1.2.1 and 26.2.1, and releases older than 20.9 must migrate to a fixed one. BleepingComputer counts it as the fifth exploited Catalyst SD-WAN zero-day of 2026. On 1 October Fortinet disclosed CVE-2026-104286 in FortiMail (FG-IR-26-175), a path-traversal and NULL-byte handling flaw that lets an unauthenticated attacker write arbitrary files on the appliance through crafted HTTP or HTTPS requests. Fortinet scores it CVSS 9.8 and says it has been reported exploited in the wild; CISA added it to KEV on 1 October with a 4 October deadline. Affected are FortiMail 7.2.0 to 7.2.9, 7.4.0 to 7.4.8, 7.6.0 to 7.6.6 and 8.0.0 to 8.0.1; Fortinet’s 5 October update lists fixed releases 7.4.9, 7.6.7 and 8.0.2, and tells 7.2 customers to move to 7.4 or later. Neither vendor has named an actor or victims, and nothing ties either flaw to rail. The rail fit is our editorial assessment: SD-WAN Manager is the controller that pushes configuration and policy to the edge routers in stations, depots, yards and wayside communication huts, so administrative access there is a route to rewriting segmentation at every site at once; FortiMail sits on the corporate side, where a compromised mail gateway can read, alter or send the messages that open most intrusions against dispatch and operations staff. - Cisco advisory cisco-sa-sdwan-webauth-xr8beuuU (revised 2 Oct 2026); Fortinet PSIRT FG-IR-26-175; CISA KEV catalogue; reported by BleepingComputer and SecurityWeek; rail relevance is our editorial assessment - Cisco advisory and KEV listing 30 Sep 2026; FortiMail disclosure and KEV listing 1 Oct 2026; Fortinet fixed-release update 5 Oct 2026

item.title: [Critical] MikroTik: the exploited “MikroTrick” SSH chain is in KEV with every deadline passed, and CISA adds a CVSS 9.8 pre-authentication web-management flaw that is not — the router class that quietly backhauls remote rail sites
item.category: Critical Advisory — Edge routers, chain confirmed exploited and KEV-listed; new pre-authentication flaw not in KEV
item.description: CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue holds three MikroTik RouterOS flaws: CVE-2026-86060, an argument-injection flaw, and CVE-2026-67277, a missing-authentication flaw in the bandwidth-test service, both added on 10 September; and CVE-2026-67279, an SSH flaw added on 25 September that lets an unauthenticated client open a session channel and send an exec request and, in KEV’s words, “can be chained to achieve unauthenticated exploitation of CVE-2026-86060”. The federal deadlines of 13 and 28 September have both passed. CERT Polska reported on 5 September that this SSH chain, which it calls MikroTrick, had been exploited in the wild since about 2 September, before patches existed, and its 22 September analysis confirms that CVE-2026-67279 combined with CVE-2026-86060 gives an unauthenticated attacker full administrative control. CVE-2026-67276, which some earlier coverage placed in the chain, is not in KEV. Fixed builds for the chain are RouterOS 7.24.2, 7.23.4 and 6.49.21, plus 7.25beta3; a related flaw, CVE-2026-67278, needs 7.24.3 or 7.23.6 because the earlier fix was incomplete. On 29 September CISA published advisory ICSA-26-272-06 for a separate flaw, CVE-2026-84411: an integer underflow in RouterOS’s HTTP request-body handling, reachable before authentication, that can give remote code execution as root, or a denial of service, from a single crafted request. It is scored CVSS v3.1 9.8 and v4 9.3, affects versions before 7.24 and is fixed from 7.24; CISA reports no known public exploitation, and it is not in KEV. Read literally, CISA’s affected range takes in the 7.23 and 6.49 builds that fix the SSH chain, so check MikroTik’s release notes before treating a device on those lines as covered. No victims, sectors or actor have been named for any of these flaws, and nothing ties the activity to rail. The relevance for this audience is our editorial assessment: low-cost RouterOS hardware, including its cellular models, is a common choice for backhaul and telemetry at remote, unstaffed sites such as crossings, wayside cabinets, yard offices and small stations, and a router compromised at that layer sits upstream of whatever segmentation you rely on. - CERT Polska advisories and its 22 Sep technical analysis; CISA KEV catalogue; CISA ICS advisory ICSA-26-272-06 (CVE-2026-84411); The Hacker News on CVE-2026-67279; no victim, sector or actor named in any source; rail relevance is our editorial assessment - CERT Polska 5 Sep 2026; KEV additions 10 Sep and 25 Sep 2026; CISA advisory ICSA-26-272-06 29 Sep 2026

item.title: [High] CISA’s 29 September and 1 October ICS batches lean on transport: a Lantronix cellular gateway whose firmware checks can be defeated, IP cameras at CVSS 10.0 with public exploit code, and an EV-charging platform with no version fix
item.category: Advisory — CISA ICS batches, transport-labelled devices, no reported exploitation
item.description: CISA published seven ICS advisories on 29 September (ICSA-26-272-01 to -07) and six on 1 October (ICSA-26-274-01 to -06), and more than half of them list Transportation Systems among the sectors using the affected products. The one closest to rail infrastructure is ICSA-26-272-01, for the Lantronix G520 Series cellular gateway: firmware 2.6.0.4R6_stable carries an improper verification of cryptographic signature flaw (CVE-2026-91191) and a cross-site scripting flaw (CVE-2026-84409), each CVSS v3.1 7.5 and v4 7.7, which CISA says could allow an attacker to replace software and execute arbitrary code with root privileges. Version 2.6.0.7R6 fixes both, and CISA names Transportation Systems, Energy, and Water and Wastewater as the sectors. ICSA-26-272-03 covers command injection in VIVOTEK camera firmware across 37 models (CVE-2026-22755, CVSS v3.1 10.0 and v4 9.3), for which public proof-of-concept code exists; the fix is current firmware. ICSA-26-274-02 covers every version of Monta’s monta.app EV-charging platform, where missing authentication on a WebSocket interface allows charging-station impersonation (CVE-2026-95102, CVSS v3.1 9.4 and v4 9.3); there is no fixed version, only Monta’s guidance to enable OCPP 1.6 Security Profile 2 and its statement that rate limiting is in place. ICSA-26-274-01 covers Armatura One physical access control below 4.7.2 (USA builds below 4.6.1), which embeds an ActiveMQ component carrying CVE-2023-46604 — a flaw already in KEV from attacks on other ActiveMQ deployments, though none is reported against Armatura — plus hard-coded keys and credentials; 4.7.2 and 4.6.1_USA fix it. The other transport-labelled items are the Viidure dashcam Android app, with hard-coded cloud credentials (CVSS 10.0) and no fix planned; two lower-scored, fixed Johnson Controls EasyIO Neo controller flaws; and Toptech TMS7 and TopHAT terminal-management software, with a CVSS 10.0 flaw fixed in 7.8. CISA reports no known exploitation for any advisory in either batch. The MikroTik advisory in the 29 September batch is covered in its own card. The rail relevance is our editorial assessment: cellular gateways of the G520 type backhaul crossings, wayside cabinets, substations and vehicle telemetry; IP cameras and access control sit in every station; and transit agencies electrifying bus fleets run depot charging platforms of exactly the Monta type. - CISA ICS advisories ICSA-26-272-01 to -07 and ICSA-26-274-01 to -06, details checked against CISA’s CSAF data as ingested by CIRCL Vulnerability-Lookup; rail relevance is our editorial assessment - Published 29 Sep 2026 and 1 Oct 2026

item.title: [Critical] Cisco Talos tracks three clusters exploiting Secure Firewall Management Center flaws CVE-2026-20079 and CVE-2026-20316 — that box is the IT/OT boundary TSA asks you to prove
item.category: Critical Advisory — Actively exploited, KEV-listed, firewall management plane
item.description: Cisco and CISA confirmed on 9 September that CVE-2026-20079 in Cisco Secure Firewall Management Center is under active exploitation. The flaw is a critical authentication bypass caused by an improper system process created at boot; a remote, unauthenticated attacker sends crafted HTTP requests and gains root on the appliance operating system. Cisco fixed it in early March and published indicators of compromise in late July, then disclosed on 9 September that it had observed exploitation from August. CISA added the CVE to KEV with a 12 September federal deadline, which has now passed. Cisco Talos tracks three clusters (its post was last revised on 21 September and still names the same three) of post-compromise activity across this flaw and the earlier CVE-2026-20316: UAT-12197, which used CVE-2026-20079 to plant a web shell and a JAR-based command executor and steal credentials; UAT-11823, an APT that used both flaws and deployed a Cyclops Blink variant, whose tooling Talos says overlaps with Sandworm’s — a tooling overlap, not an attribution: Talos does not attribute this activity to Sandworm; and UAT-11988, which Talos assesses with high confidence to be a ransomware operator with TTPs consistent with Qilin affiliates; Talos ties its access to CVE-2026-20316 (static credentials), not to CVE-2026-20079, and it deployed Qilin on selected endpoints. CVE-2026-20316 is not in the KEV catalogue. On 16 September Cisco shipped its September hardening release for ASA, FTD and FMC (CVE-2026-20329 to CVE-2026-20336, maximum CVSS 9.9), and revised the FMC advisory to replace the earlier hot fixes with those security-hardening builds (7.0.10, 7.2.12, 7.4.8, 7.6.6, 7.7.13, 10.0.2 and 10.1.0); there is no workaround. Talos’s post was last revised on 21 September, and nothing rail-specific has been reported. For railroads and transit agencies the consequence is specific. TSA security directives require a documented, tested separation between IT and critical cyber systems — dispatch, signalling support, traction-power SCADA, fare and station systems. FMC is where that separation is enforced, and root there lets an attacker edit it silently. - Cisco security advisory update and Cisco Talos research of 9 Sep 2026, plus the CISA KEV addition of 9 Sep 2026 — reported by SecurityWeek; Talos cluster wording re-checked against the Talos post (revised 21 Sep 2026) on 22 Sep 2026 - Advisory updated and KEV listing added 9 Sep 2026; reporting 10 Sep 2026; hardening release published 16 Sep 2026; KEV status re-checked 22 Sep 2026; no new development found as of 27 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] Four more boundary products went into KEV on 22 September — Check Point VPN and management, Arista’s SD-WAN orchestrator and F5 APM, and the 25 September deadline has passed
item.category: Critical Advisory — Actively exploited, KEV-listed, network edge and management plane
item.description: CISA added four actively exploited flaws to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on 22 September, each with a federal remediation deadline of 25 September. Two are Check Point’s, confirmed in Check Point’s own advisories; neither Check Point nor the reporting gives a CVSS score, and we do not supply one. CVE-2026-85102 is improper certificate validation on Security Gateways and Spark firewalls running Site-to-Site or Remote Access VPN, giving unauthenticated remote code execution; patches shipped on 9 September and exploitation has been observed from 12 September. CVE-2026-93616 is a separate, pre-authentication path traversal affecting Security Management and Multi-Domain servers, log servers and SmartEvent that lets an attacker upload and execute scripts; Check Point says it was exploited as a zero-day in a handful of pinpointed attacks on 23 July. The third is Arista VeloCloud Orchestrator, CVE-2026-93952 (CVSS v3.1 10.0, v4.0 9.5), an input-validation flaw in on-premises orchestrators that Arista says is actively exploited; exposure requires certificate-based Edge-to-Orchestrator authentication, and hosted orchestrators are already patched. The fourth is F5 BIG-IP APM, CVE-2026-94127 (CVSS v3.1 9.8, v4.0 9.3), an unauthenticated heap overflow reachable only where a virtual server combines an APM access policy with an OAuth profile, fixed by engineering hotfixes; CISA and F5 advise applying F5’s iRule first, to allow forensic triage, and then the hotfix. No victim in any sector has been named and nothing ties these to rail. The rail fit is architectural: SD-WAN orchestrators push configuration to the edges in stations, depots and wayside communication huts; Check Point gateways often terminate supplier remote access; and the management server holds the policy that enforces the IT/OT separation TSA asks you to document. - CISA KEV alert of 22 Sep 2026; Check Point security advisory (22 Sep 2026); Arista Security Advisory 0183; F5 K000162605 as summarised by Rapid7; rail relevance is our editorial assessment - Added to KEV 22 Sep 2026; federal remediation deadline 25 Sep 2026, now passed; no new development found as of 27 Sep 2026

item.title: [High] A CVSS 9.8 flaw in the lwIP embedded network stack leads CISA’s 22 September batch — the question is which of your field devices ship its MQTT client
item.category: Advisory — CISA ICS batch, embedded TCP/IP stack, no reported exploitation
item.description: CISA published nine ICS advisories on 22 September: two for lwIP, the lightweight open-source TCP/IP stack built into a very wide range of embedded controllers, gateways, I/O modules and sensors; six for Siemens; and one for OpenPLC. The headline is ICSA-26-265-01, an out-of-bounds write in lwIP’s MQTT client application (CVE-2026-87121, CVSS 9.8 v3.1 and 9.3 v4.0, network-reachable with no authentication or user interaction) that may give an attacker full code execution on the device; it was reported by Shahriyar Jalayeri of ByteRay. ICSA-26-265-02 is a separate double free in lwIP, reported by Eric Evenchick of Tetrel Security; we could not verify its CVE or score, so none is quoted. Because lwIP is a library, the practical exposure depends on which device vendors compiled in the MQTT client, and no downstream vendor list had been published by 24 September. Two of the Siemens advisories touch station estates: an unrestricted file upload in Siveillance Control, Siemens’ physical-security management platform, and a code-injection flaw in the Desigo CC building-management family, reported by Michelin CERT. No exploitation is reported for any advisory in the batch. For rail, the plausible lwIP carriers are the telemetry gateways, condition-monitoring sensors and small controllers in traction-power, tunnel-ventilation and wayside cabinets, many of which publish over MQTT. - CISA ICS advisories ICSA-26-265-01 and -02 and the 22 Sep 2026 batch, as listed by Chemical Facility Security News; CVSS for CVE-2026-87121 per the published CVE record (Ubuntu CVE tracker); rail-device relevance is our editorial assessment - Published 22 Sep 2026

item.title: [High] CISA adds a Zyxel GS1900 switch flaw to KEV after GreyNoise counts 996 compromised units — the kind of switch found in a station office, not a signal room
item.category: Advisory — Actively exploited, KEV-listed, small-office switch
item.description: CISA added CVE-2026-7273 to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on 21 September with a federal remediation deadline of 24 September. It is a stack-based buffer overflow in the CGI program of Zyxel GS1900-series managed switches (GS1900-8, 8HP, 10HP, 16, 24, 24E, 24EP, 24HPv2, 48 and 48HPv2) that lets an unauthenticated attacker with access to the management interface execute operating-system commands through a crafted HTTP request. Zyxel published the fix in June; its advisory gives no CVSS score and we do not supply one. On 21 September GreyNoise published what it describes as the first documented in-the-wild exploitation: a single actor, assessed by GreyNoise as Chinese-speaking, has compromised 996 GS1900 switches across 48 countries since about mid-August, including 129 in the United States and 66 in the Netherlands, using an obfuscated Python tool that pulled device configurations and root-level password hashes over TFTP; 564 of the victims were still on factory-default credentials. GreyNoise links the same actor to data theft from an unnamed western government organisation through two WordPress flaws, and describes it as related to, or the same as, the actor behind earlier Gitea exploitation — an inference, not an observation. No rail or transit victim is identified. Our assessment of the rail relevance: GS1900 is a small-office switch, and the place it turns up on a railway or transit property is the station back office, the yard office, the small agency’s headquarters LAN or a contractor’s site cabin, not the signalling or traction-power network. A compromised switch there yields a network foothold and every credential configured on it. - CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue (21 Sep 2026 update), GreyNoise research of 21 Sep 2026 and Zyxel’s June 2026 advisory; rail relevance is our editorial assessment - Added to KEV 21 Sep 2026; GreyNoise report 21 Sep 2026; Zyxel fix published Jun 2026

item.title: [High] Three exploited Linux kernel flaws land in KEV with a three-day federal deadline — the question for rail is which appliances run Linux underneath
item.category: Advisory — Three additions to the CISA KEV catalogue
item.description: CISA added three Linux kernel vulnerabilities to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on 18 September, across two alerts, with a federal remediation deadline of 21 September, which has now passed; no further exploitation detail has been published since the listing. CVE-2025-39682 is in the kernel TLS receive path, where a zero-length record can bypass record-type handling. CVE-2026-53266 is an out-of-bounds write in the netfilter bridge ebtables SNAT target, which can lead to memory corruption, denial of service or local privilege escalation on hosts with bridge netfilter rules configured. CVE-2025-39964 is a race condition in the AF_ALG crypto socket interface, exploitable by a local, low-privileged user. Published severity scores for the three differ widely between sources, so none is quoted here. CISA lists them as exploited in the wild, but no public detail says who is exploiting them or against what, and none is tied to a rail or OT target. None is a rail product. As with the Linux kernel addition of 27 August, the relevance is that traffic-management servers, passenger information systems, CCTV recorders and many wayside and on-board gateways run Linux underneath, often as vendor appliances patched on the supplier’s schedule. These are local, post-access bugs that let an attacker who already has a foothold go further, not ways in from the internet. - CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue (18 Sep 2026 update) and CISA alerts of 18 Sep 2026, with reporting by The Hacker News; rail relevance is our editorial assessment - Added to KEV 18 Sep 2026; federal remediation deadline 21 Sep 2026, passed; status re-checked 22 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] A CVSS 10.0 authentication bypass in Cisco Identity Services Engine is being exploited — that is the box deciding who gets onto which network
item.category: Critical Advisory — Actively exploited, KEV-listed
item.description: Cisco published advisory cisco-sa-ISE-ABP-VNSW7Tn5 on 16 September for CVE-2026-76460, a CVSS 10.0 flaw in Identity Services Engine and ISE-PIC. An API endpoint with insufficient authentication lets a remote, unauthenticated attacker bypass the web-based management interface, and Cisco states that its PSIRT is aware of active exploitation. All versions are affected; fixes are 3.1 Patch 12, 3.2 Patch 11, 3.3 Patch 12, 3.4 Patch 7 and 3.5 Patch 4. There are no workarounds — restricting management traffic with infrastructure access control lists is the only mitigation Cisco offers. CISA added the CVE to the KEV catalogue on 16 September with a three-day federal deadline of 19 September, which has now passed. No actor attribution has been published, and no critical-infrastructure or OT targeting has been claimed; Singapore’s Cyber Security Agency reinforced the advisory with its own alert on 21 September. ISE 3.0 is end-of-life and gets no fix, so those deployments must migrate. The rail relevance is structural rather than reported: ISE is the network access control and policy engine many railroads and transit authorities use to decide which port, VLAN and remote session a device or contractor is allowed, including the segmentation between corporate systems and dispatch, signalling support, traction-power SCADA and station estates. Root over the policy engine is root over the boundary. Separately, CISA added Cisco Secure Email Gateway CVE-2026-76461 to KEV on 14 September, due 17 September — a second exploited Cisco entry point in the same week. - Cisco security advisory cisco-sa-ISE-ABP-VNSW7Tn5 and the CISA KEV catalogue — corroborated by SecurityWeek and BleepingComputer - Advisory published and KEV listing added 16 Sep 2026; federal deadline 19 Sep 2026 passed; status re-checked 22 Sep 2026

item.title: [Medium] Moxa fixes an unauthenticated crash in the web login of its TN-4500B switches — a line it markets for rolling-stock networks
item.category: Advisory — On-board train Ethernet switch, availability only
item.description: Moxa published security advisory MPSA-252620 on 18 September for CVE-2026-15579 in its TN-4500B Ethernet switch series, a line Moxa markets for rolling-stock networks: its product page describes the ToughNet TN-4500B switches as designed for railway applications including rolling stock, and as meeting the EN 50155 test requirements. The flaw is an out-of-bounds write (CWE-787) in the web login: the username field is not length-checked, so a remote, unauthenticated attacker who can reach the web interface can send an overlong value and crash the authentication process. The impact Moxa describes is denial of service, with no confidentiality loss; it scores the flaw CVSS v4 8.8 (vector AV:N/AC:L/AT:N/PR:N/UI:N/VC:N/VI:L/VA:H) and rates it High. Firmware v2.0 and earlier is affected and v2.1 or later fixes it. The advisory makes no statement about exploitation, and we found no report of attacks. Our assessment of the rail relevance: switches of this class usually sit inside the train, carrying the on-board network, so the reachable question is which vehicle networks and train-to-ground links expose the switch’s web management at all. - Moxa security advisory MPSA-252620 (CVE-2026-15579, credited to Mask Lu); product description from Moxa’s TN-4500B Series page; rail-network relevance is our editorial assessment - Advisory published 18 Sep 2026

item.title: [High] Twenty flaws in Pepperl+Fuchs IO-Link masters, two of them CVSS 9.8 and unauthenticated — the same CVE set appears under Phoenix Contact and Carlo Gavazzi badges, and Nozomi has now published the attack chain
item.category: Advisory — Vendor firmware fix, CVSS 9.8, no reported exploitation
item.description: CERT@VDE published VDE-2026-014 on 16 September for 20 vulnerabilities (CVE-2026-27546 to CVE-2026-27565) in the firmware of Pepperl+Fuchs ICE2-8IOL and ICE3-8IOL IO-Link master modules, found by Nozomi Networks researchers. Firmware below 1.7.4 is affected and 1.7.8 fixes them. The two worst are CVE-2026-27546, an authentication bypass, and CVE-2026-27565, an unauthenticated upload of a malicious IODD device-description file that executes shell scripts, both CVSS v3.1 9.8. The remainder (CVE-2026-27547 to -27564) are command-injection, file-inclusion and authorisation flaws between 7.2 and 8.8 that lead to root-level code execution; CVE-2026-27557 (7.5) is an unauthenticated path traversal that reads the SSH server’s private keys, and CVE-2026-27553 (6.5) discloses password hashes. With the same CVE set, Phoenix Contact IOL MA8 PN DI8 and IOL MA8 EIP DI8 modules (VDE-2026-027, 20 CVEs) and Carlo Gavazzi YL212 and YN115 masters (VDE-2026-028) carry the same fixes on the same date. On 24 September Nozomi Networks Labs published its technical write-up of the Pepperl+Fuchs findings, tested on an ICE2-8IOL-K45P-RJ45 running EtherNet/IP firmware 1.7.3: it counts 19 CVEs on that module and shows that, chained, they give an unauthenticated attacker root on the device and the ability to manipulate sensor and actuator data. No exploitation is reported, and no CISA ICS advisory had covered the flaws through CISA’s 1 October batch. The rail relevance is our assessment rather than anything in the advisory: IO-Link masters sit at the sensor and actuator layer of discrete automation, which on a railway means depot and workshop equipment, wheel lathes, wash plants, material-handling and platform plant supplied by integrators, usually on PROFINET or EtherNet/IP segments the operator’s IT team has never inventoried. Nothing here touches signalling or train control. - CERT@VDE advisory VDE-2026-014 (Pepperl+Fuchs), with VDE-2026-027 (Phoenix Contact) and VDE-2026-028 (Carlo Gavazzi); Nozomi Networks Labs technical write-up; rail-estate relevance is our editorial assessment - CERT@VDE advisories 16 Sep 2026; Nozomi write-up 24 Sep 2026

item.title: [Medium] Seven new ICS advisories and one update on 17 September — one of them a transport device, none of them exploited
item.category: Advisory — CISA ICS batch, no reported exploitation
item.description: CISA published seven new advisories, ICSA-26-260-01 through -07, plus one update, on Thursday 17 September; the next batch followed on 22 September and is carried as a separate card. The advisory carrying CISA’s Transportation Systems label is ICSA-26-260-01, covering Bransys ELD for Android below 11.00.00 and for iOS below 1.1.54: hard-coded MQTT credentials (CVE-2026-86520, CVSS 7.5), cleartext transmission of sensitive information (CVE-2026-86689, 5.9) and hard-coded FTP credentials (CVE-2026-77960, 5.3), all fixed in the versions named. These are electronic logging devices for commercial road vehicles, so for a railroad or transit authority the exposure sits with fleet, maintenance-of-way and non-revenue vehicle telematics rather than anywhere near train control — it should not be read as a rail advisory. The most significant score in the batch is ICSA-26-260-02, a Mitsubishi Electric authentication-algorithm flaw in GX Works3 and Motion Control Settings affecting all versions (CVE-2026-15688, CVSS 8.8 v3.1 and 8.7 v4.0), which allows a local authentication bypass and tampering with control programs — relevant to workshop, depot and maintenance-facility automation. The remaining five cover Hitachi Energy FACTS Control Platform (-03, whose score we could not verify, so none is quoted), Schneider Electric Modicon M340 and X80 Ethernet communication modules (-04, CVE-2025-6625, a denial of service through a crafted FTP command, CVSS 7.5 v3.1 and 8.7 v4, fixed in M340 firmware SV3.70; a republication of Schneider’s 2025 advisory), Schneider Electric NetBotz 5 750 and 755 (-05, CVE-2026-13336 command injection at 6.4 v3.1 and 7.3 v4, plus CVE-2026-13337, fixed in 5.6.0), ABB Ability Edgenius (-06, the “Copy Fail” Linux kernel flaw CVE-2026-31431 at 7.8, fixed in 3.2.4.1) and Schneider Electric PowerChute Serial Shutdown (-07, CVE-2026-13348, excessive authentication attempts, 5.3 v3.1 and 6.9 v4; see the vendor advisory for the fixed version). CISA also updated ICSA-26-211-07 (Mitsubishi CC-Link IE TSN) on 17 September to add eight affected products. No exploitation is reported for anything in the batch. - CISA ICS advisories ICSA-26-260-01 to -07 and the update to ICSA-26-211-07 — scores for -01 and -04 to -07 checked against CISA’s CSAF files 20 Sep 2026 and re-checked 22 Sep 2026; -03 unscored and deliberately not quoted - Published 17 Sep 2026

item.title: [Medium] Rockwell extends its lockout-recovery guidance to Micro820 and Micro850 — the small PLCs attackers were found setting passwords on
item.category: Advisory — Vendor hardening and recovery guidance, revised
item.description: Rockwell Automation published revision 5.0 of security notice SD1790 on 18 September, its fifth revision since the notice first appeared on 30 July. The notice exists because of an FBI public service announcement of 30 July describing attackers who remotely altered the configuration of internet-exposed programmable logic controllers, changed IP addresses and set passwords where none had existed, locking the operators out. The original guidance covered MicroLogix 1100 and 1400; revision 5.0 extends the hardening and password-recovery instructions to the Micro820 and Micro850 controllers as well. There is no CVE: the notice is about exposure and configuration, not a software flaw. The controls Rockwell lists are the familiar ones — remove the controller from any internet-reachable path, put access behind a VPN and firewall, set strong passwords, keep offline backups of the project so a locked controller can be restored, disable the built-in HTTP server and keep firmware current. The revision adds no new incident data. Our assessment of the rail relevance: MicroLogix and Micro800-class controllers are the low-cost PLCs that end up in small, distributed installations built by contractors — pump and drainage stations, tunnel and station plant, yard equipment, small traction-power auxiliaries — often with a cellular modem for remote support and no entry in the operator’s OT asset register. The FBI describes a class of attack that needs no exploit at all, just reachability. - Rockwell Automation security notice SD1790 revision 5.0, referencing the FBI public service announcement of 30 Jul 2026; rail installation pattern is our editorial assessment - Revision 5.0 published 18 Sep 2026; original notice 30 Jul 2026

item.title: [Critical] ConnectWise ScreenConnect joins KEV with attackers already pushing scripts to endpoints as they connect — the second remote-support console in five days
item.category: Critical Advisory — Actively exploited, KEV-listed, remote support
item.description: CISA added CVE-2026-84869 to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on 11 September. It is a missing-authorisation flaw in ConnectWise ScreenConnect, scored CVSS 9.9, that permits unauthorised file transfer and code execution, and three separate incidents are documented in which threat actors abused it to push malicious scripts to endpoints at the moment those endpoints connected. A patch is available and the federal remediation deadline was 14 September. Arriving five days after N-able N-central landed in the same catalogue at CVSS 10.0, this is the same failure twice inside a week, in the two consoles third parties most often use to reach industrial estates. ScreenConnect in particular travels in the field-service bag: signalling contractors, fare-collection vendors, SCADA integrators and building-systems suppliers install it to support what they commissioned, frequently without a change record, and frequently on machines that also talk to the operational network. - CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue addition of 11 Sep 2026, with the ConnectWise advisory — reported by The Hacker News - Added to KEV 11 Sep 2026; federal remediation deadline 14 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] GitLab CVSS 10 path traversal is being exploited, and rail and transit teams host more of it than they think
item.category: Advisory — Actively exploited, CISA KEV
item.description: GitLab patched CVE-2026-85706 on 10 September, a path-traversal flaw in the repository commits API that it rated CVSS 10.0 and that allows an unauthenticated attacker to read arbitrary files from a GitLab server. CISA added it to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on Friday 11 September with a remediation deadline for federal agencies of Monday 14 September. watchTowr reported it was already seeing in-the-wild probes for vulnerable servers, and Hong Kong’s CERT issued its own advisory on 14 September stating the flaw is being exploited in the wild. A second flaw fixed in the same release, CVE-2026-87719, can expose sensitive information from Enterprise Edition servers. Passenger and freight operators keep dispatch, CAD/AVL, passenger-information, fare-collection and back-office signalling support code in self-hosted GitLab instances that often sit on the corporate side with routed paths into the operational network. Unauthenticated file reads expose the credentials and integration detail that bridge those two worlds. - GitLab patch release advisory and CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog — reporting via Cybersecurity Dive - GitLab patch published 10 Sep 2026; KEV listing 11 Sep 2026; reporting 14 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] CISA flags a CVSS 9.8 missing-authorisation flaw in mySCADA myPRO Manager — and lists Transportation among the sectors running it
item.category: Critical Advisory — SCADA/HMI management, unexploited
item.description: CISA published ICSA-26-258-03 on 15 September covering mySCADA myPRO Manager version 2.1 and earlier. It carries two flaws: CVE-2026-73807, a missing-authorisation vulnerability scored CVSS v3 9.8, and CVE-2026-82567, missing authentication for a critical function, scored 6.3. Together they could let an attacker reach privileged management functions or send arbitrary SMS messages through a GSM modem connected to the system. mySCADA has fixed both in version 2.2. CISA lists the deployed sectors as Critical Manufacturing, Energy, Food and Agriculture, Transportation and Water, and states that no known public exploitation targeting these flaws has been reported to it. No rail or transit deployment is named in the advisory. The relevance here is inventory: small SCADA and HMI packages turn up in station plant, pumping, tunnel ventilation and depot systems commissioned by integrators, and an SMS-capable modem on such a system is often the alarm path to on-call staff. - CISA ICS advisory ICSA-26-258-03 - Published 15 Sep 2026

item.title: [High] Nozomi’s SCALANCE LPE9403 research now runs to twelve flaws, several chainable to root on an OT edge device — vendor-patched and unexploited
item.category: Advisory — Vendor patch, vulnerability research
item.description: Nozomi Networks Labs published the second part of its Siemens SCALANCE LPE9403 research on 18 September, taking the disclosed set to twelve vulnerabilities: nine in the device firmware, scored CVSS 5.3 to 8.5, and three in the SINEMA Remote Connect Edge Client, scored 6.7 to 8.5. The first part, published 10 September, covered four memory-corruption flaws in the PROFINET Discovery and basic Configuration Protocol implementation — CVE-2025-40575 through CVE-2025-40578, each CVSS 5.3 — where a daemon running as root, unauthenticated and bound to every device interface can be crashed with crafted Ethernet frames from the same Layer 2 segment. The material addition in part two is that Nozomi demonstrates several of the flaws chaining to root-level control of the device, which would allow telemetry to be manipulated, alarms suppressed, operational data read, OT services disrupted and lateral movement attempted from the edge node. This is disclosed research on vendor-patched issues rather than a new critical exposure: the CVEs carry 2025 identifiers, Siemens has published fixes, the affected versions are LPE9403 firmware below V4.0 HF0 and SINEMA Remote Connect Edge Client through V2.1, and CISA’s update of the existing advisory ICSA-25-135-18 to version 4 on 15 September added the Edge Client and the vendor fixes. There is no evidence of exploitation in the wild. Rail and transit estates running the LPE9403 as an edge processing node in depots, traction power rooms or station plant rooms should treat this as a firmware-currency question: the realistic worst case is not a crash but an edge device that keeps reporting normally while under someone else’s control. - Nozomi Networks Labs research, parts one and two, and Siemens ProductCERT SSA-327438 — reporting via Industrial Cyber; CISA advisory ICSA-25-135-18 updated to version 4 - Nozomi research 10 Sep 2026 and 18 Sep 2026; CISA advisory update 15 Sep 2026; CVEs originally disclosed May 2025 under ICSA-25-135-18

item.title: [Critical] N-able N-central lands in KEV at CVSS 10 — the console many transit and short-line IT providers run
item.category: Critical Advisory — Actively exploited, KEV-listed
item.description: CISA added four actively exploited vulnerabilities to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 8 September. The lead item is CVE-2026-86218 in N-able N-central, a static code injection flaw scored CVSS 10.0 that yields pre-authentication remote code execution. N-able confirmed exploitation in the wild, Huntress observed attacks against N-central’s API and appliance logs from 4 September, and N-able shipped 2026.3 Hotfix 4 on 5 September — its fourth hotfix in five weeks. The federal remediation deadline was 11 September and has now passed. N-central is a remote monitoring and management platform: an agent with system-level rights on every managed endpoint, operated by a third party. Short lines, commuter authorities and municipal transit agencies commonly outsource back-office IT to providers running exactly this console. Also added were two Windows zero-days granting SYSTEM and an Adobe Commerce injection flaw. - CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog addition of 8 Sep 2026, with N-able and Huntress reporting — corroborated by BleepingComputer and SecurityWeek - Added to KEV 8 Sep 2026; vendor hotfix released 5 Sep 2026; federal remediation deadline 11 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] NetScaler and FortiOS are confirmed exploited and in KEV — the two boxes most often standing between a supplier and a rail OT network
item.category: Critical Advisory — Actively exploited, KEV-listed, network edge
item.description: CISA added two more edge products to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on 9 September. The first is an authentication bypass in Citrix NetScaler ADC and NetScaler Gateway, CVE-2026-19490 at CVSS 9.3, affecting AAA virtual server and Gateway configurations; honeypot telemetry recorded 56 exploitation attempts from 3 September, 36 of them on 8 September alone. The second is a heap buffer overflow in Fortinet FortiOS, FortiSwitchManager and FortiSASE, CVE-2025-25249 at CVSS 7.3, exploited since July 2026 in a campaign distributing the PivotC2 remote access trojan that has reached more than 3,000 addresses, with an estimated 178 FortiGate devices found infected and the concentration in the United States. Both carried a federal remediation deadline of 12 September, now passed. Three further NetScaler zero-days followed from 27 September; they are carried in their own card above. Neither of these is an IT asset in any useful sense for a railroad: the NetScaler gateway is how the signalling supplier gets in, and the FortiGate is often the only device between the corporate network and a dispatch or SCADA segment. - CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue additions of 9 Sep 2026, with Citrix and Fortinet advisories — reported by The Hacker News - Added to KEV 9 Sep 2026; federal remediation deadline 12 Sep 2026; FortiOS exploitation traced to July 2026

item.title: [Critical] September’s ICS patch round lands on Modicon controllers, RTUs and the protection relays behind traction power
item.category: Critical Advisory — September ICS Patch Tuesday, controllers and protection relays
item.description: Schneider Electric published four advisories on 8 September, the most severe a critical authentication vulnerability in the Modicon M580 and Modicon M580 Safety controllers, CVE-2026-3869 at CVSS v4.0 9.2 (v3.1 9.8). Also fixed: high-severity flaws in the PowerLogic T300 RTU — formerly the Easergy T300, a distribution-automation RTU that turns up in traction-power and substation retrofits — and in EcoStruxure IT Data Center Expert, plus a medium-severity SCADAPack x70 defect. Siemens issued nine advisories, seven on 8 September, headlined by ProductCERT SSA-142885: fourteen CVEs in Reyrolle 7SR5 protection and control relays for all versions before V2.70, led by CVE-2026-62645 (CVSS v3.1 9.8), where the web interface leaks enough data to calculate current and past session identifiers and bypass authentication. Siemens also patched Industrial Edge Management and Open Interface Services, and Aveva fixed four flaws in the PIMBoards component of Pipeline Integrity Monitor, which CISA published on 10 September as ICSA-26-253-01: a hardcoded cryptographic key (CVE-2026-81821) and a weak password-hashing algorithm (CVE-2026-81822), both CVSS v3 8.4, plus a missing-authorisation flaw (CVE-2026-81823, 5.3) and a cross-site scripting flaw (CVE-2026-81824, 4.7), all fixed in 2025 SP1 P2. That product is an oil-and-gas pipeline leak-detection tool rather than a rail one, and is listed here for completeness of the September round. CISA republished the Reyrolle 7SR5 advisory as ICSA-26-258-05 and the SCADAPack x70 advisory as ICSA-26-258-04 on 15 September. No exploitation is reported for any of it. - Siemens ProductCERT SSA-142885 and the September Schneider Electric and Aveva security advisories — round-up via SecurityWeek - Vendor advisories published 8 Sep 2026; CISA advisory ICSA-26-253-01 covering the Aveva flaws published 10 Sep 2026; Reyrolle 7SR5 and SCADAPack x70 republished by CISA 15 Sep 2026

item.title: [Info] The OT Cybersecurity Coalition asks CISA for a binding directive on federal agencies’ own OT — a proposal, landing days after GAO found only 7 of 22 civilian agencies fully meet the device rules already in place
item.category: Regulation & Policy — Industry proposal for a federal OT directive; GAO audit
item.description: The OT Cybersecurity Coalition, an industry group, published a paper on 6 October, reported by CyberScoop, urging CISA to issue a binding operational directive dedicated to operational technology at federal civilian agencies. It asks that the directive make each agency assign an accountable OT cybersecurity officer, set minimum practices drawn from existing federal guidance, align with CISA’s 2022 Cross-Sector Cybersecurity Performance Goals, and consider whether past NSA OT guidance should apply to civilian agencies. In the coalition’s words, “it is time for an encompassing BOD solely focused on OT security.” Earlier directives (BOD 23-01, 23-02 and 26-04) touched OT without being dedicated to it. The coalition cites GAO-26-108937, published on 30 September, which reviewed 22 civilian CFO Act agencies against OMB requirements for networked IoT and OT devices: 15 had established inventories, 11 maintained them, 10 included all required information, and only 7 fully met all three. GAO notes that OMB has yet to issue updated guidance covering fiscal year 2026 and recommends that it do so. CISA did not respond to CyberScoop and has announced no such directive. A directive of this kind would bind federal civilian agencies only — not railroads, transit authorities or their contractors. The rail relevance is our editorial assessment: federal directives tend to become the reference for what regulators and auditors later expect of operators, and the requirements the coalition lists — a named OT owner, an inventory that is maintained rather than compiled once, minimum practices tied to the performance goals — are the ones TSA assessments already probe. - OT Cybersecurity Coalition paper as reported by CyberScoop; GAO-26-108937; rail relevance is our editorial assessment - GAO report 30 Sep 2026; coalition paper 6 Oct 2026

item.title: [Info] CISA’s “Securing the Next 250” campaign boils critical-infrastructure advice down to reduce, replace, recover — and “replace” means the end-of-support kit railways keep longest
item.category: Regulation & Policy — CISA awareness campaign, voluntary
item.description: CISA has launched Securing the Next 250 for Cybersecurity Awareness Month, a voluntary campaign aimed at critical-infrastructure owners and operators, state and local governments and individuals, reported by Industrial Cyber on 2 October. Its organising idea is three Rs: reduce attack surfaces, replace end-of-support devices, and recover quickly to sustain operations. For individuals it repeats four practices: avoid and report phishing, use strong and unique passwords, turn on multifactor authentication and password managers, and keep software updated. Acting Director Nick Andersen framed the campaign around the knock-on effect a disruption has on the businesses and communities that depend on vital services. The campaign creates no new obligation and does not single out transportation. It is here because the three Rs map unusually well onto rail estates, where equipment lifecycles run to decades: reduce is the internet-facing remote-access and edge gear driving this page’s threat level, replace is the unsupported operating systems and network devices left in signalling support, passenger information and station plant, and recover is the manual-working plan that keeps trains moving when those systems are lost. That reading is our editorial assessment. - CISA Cybersecurity Awareness Month campaign, as reported by Industrial Cyber; rail relevance is our editorial assessment - Reported 2 Oct 2026

item.title: [Info] GAO’s industry panel says overlapping cyber-reporting rules pull responders away from containment — and CIRCIA’s final rule has missed its September target
item.category: Regulation & Policy — Incident reporting burden, GAO panel report
item.description: GAO published GAO-26-109197 on 28 September, Cybersecurity Regulations: Industry Panelists Identify Duplication and Conflicts and Ways to Address Them. It records a virtual panel held on 16 July 2026 with six industry representatives from energy, financial services, and healthcare and public health, who said it could be difficult to satisfy every reporting requirement while also remediating a threat, and who saw DHS and SEC rules as duplicating sector-specific ones. Half of the participants agreed that progress on harmonisation has been limited. Their suggestions were consistent timeframes, thresholds and definitions; a lead agency such as CISA to coordinate reporting; and closer government–industry collaboration. The report makes no formal GAO recommendations, and no rail or transit participant is listed. It follows analysis published on 8 September by the McCrary Institute and the US Chamber of Commerce, citing earlier GAO work, that counted 117 federal cyber incident reporting regulations across 27 agencies, 48 of which reach private industry. The rule that would add another federal clock, CISA’s CIRCIA final rule, was targeted in the federal regulatory agenda for September 2026; as of 6 October it had not been published in the Federal Register, so its 72-hour incident and 24-hour ransom-payment reporting duties are not yet in force. Rail sits in an unusually crowded corner of this map: a single event at a transit authority can trigger the 72-hour report to CISA required under the TSA security directives, an FTA or state safety oversight notification, a local emergency-management report and a breach notification if rider or payment data is involved — and, once it is final, CIRCIA as well. - GAO-26-109197; McCrary Institute and US Chamber of Commerce analysis via Industrial Cyber; CIRCIA status from the Federal Register; rail relevance is our editorial assessment - GAO report 28 Sep 2026; McCrary analysis 8 Sep 2026

item.title: [Info] CISA and the FBI say an automation integrator serving power and transportation customers lost about 800 files of their SCADA data — your signalling contractor holds the same kind of files
item.category: Regulation & Policy — CISA and FBI joint fact sheet on third-party ICS integrator risk; transportation named; no CVE
item.description: The FBI and CISA publicised a joint fact sheet on 24 September (the document itself is dated 23 September), “Considerations for Critical Infrastructure Operators Working With Third-Party ICS Integrators”. It is built around a 2025 case: in March and April of that year, foreign cyber actors accessed a US industrial automation solutions company that provided system integration, engineering consulting and SCADA programming services to power utilities and transportation entities, and packaged customer SCADA information, ICS device details and schematics — roughly 800 files — into nine archive files. The agencies do not name the integrator, its customers or the actor, and describe no follow-on disruption. The core recommendation is the principle of least privilege for every integrator connection, with secure, operator-controlled remote access, an inventory of the data and hardware each integrator can reach, minimal internet exposure, cybersecurity requirements in contracts, and offline backups with the ability to operate manually. For rail the fit is direct: signalling, communications, SCADA and passenger-information projects are almost always delivered by integrators, whose own servers hold your design documents, configurations and credentials long after commissioning. - FBI and CISA joint fact sheet (IC3 document) — reported by Industrial Cyber and SecurityWeek; the CISA page could not be fetched directly; rail relevance is our editorial assessment - Document dated 23 Sep 2026; publicised 24 Sep 2026

item.title: [Info] NIST’s draft SP 800-82 Rev. 4 adds freight rail to the federal OT security guide — comments are open until 30 November
item.category: Regulation & Policy — NIST draft OT security guide, freight rail newly in scope, comments due 30 Nov 2026
item.description: NIST released the initial public draft of SP 800-82 Revision 4, “Guide to Operational Technology (OT) Security”, on 21 September, with public comments open through 30 November 2026. The revision restructures the guide around the NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0, refocusing its risk material on the Govern function, and expands guidance on asset management, network monitoring and zero-trust architecture. It also adds sector coverage the guide did not previously carry: building automation, water and wastewater, food and agriculture, maritime vessels, IIoT and cloud convergence — and freight rail. The draft is guidance, not regulation, and places no new obligation on any railroad. The rail relevance is our editorial assessment: SP 800-82 is the reference many US OT programmes, auditors and integrators cite, so its freight rail material is likely to shape what assessors and contracts treat as good practice, and the draft stage is when operators can correct it. - NIST Computer Security Resource Center (initial public draft); reported by SecurityWeek; rail relevance is our editorial assessment - Draft released 21 Sep 2026; comments due 30 Nov 2026

item.title: [Info] CISA’s Cyber Storm X put a nation-state attack on rail and ports at the centre of the national exercise — the after-action report is the part worth waiting for
item.category: Regulation & Policy — National exercise, transportation and water
item.description: CISA announced on 22 September that it had run Cyber Storm X, the tenth in its national cyber exercise series: four days, about 2,000 participants from more than 200 federal, state, local and private-sector organisations, built around a nation-state adversary targeting the transportation systems sector, with rail and ports named, and the water and wastewater sector. The stated objectives were to test response plans, practise coordination and information sharing, and examine roles and responsibilities under national-level cyber plans. Acting CISA Director Nick Andersen said exercises make sure “our plans, policies, and partnerships are ready when we need them.” CISA says it will publish a public after-action report with observations, analyses and recommendations. The exercise dates were not given in the coverage we could read. This is preparedness, not an incident, and it does not move the threat level on this page; it is here because a scenario that places rail inside a national nation-state playbook is the closest thing to sector-specific federal attention in September. - CISA news release on Cyber Storm X — reported by Industrial Cyber (the CISA page could not be fetched directly) - Announced and reported 22 Sep 2026; exercise dates not stated; after-action report to follow

item.title: [Info] ENISA switches on the Single Reporting Platform as the Cyber Resilience Act’s vulnerability reporting duties take effect
item.category: Regulation & Policy — EU Cyber Resilience Act
item.description: The EU Agency for Cybersecurity deployed the initial operating capability of its Single Reporting Platform, announced 14 September, giving manufacturers and open-source software stewards the channel they need to meet Cyber Resilience Act reporting obligations that took effect in September. Under the CRA, makers of products with digital elements must report actively exploited vulnerabilities and severe incidents on a defined clock, with an early warning followed by a fuller notification. Rail operators are largely beneficiaries rather than regulated parties, but rolling-stock, signalling and passenger-system suppliers selling into the EU now carry the reporting duty, and their disclosure timelines should tighten accordingly. Reported here factually as a regulatory milestone, without comment on the underlying policy debate. - ENISA announcement of the Single Reporting Platform initial operating capability — reporting via Industrial Cyber - Announced and reported 14 Sep 2026; CRA reporting obligations effective September 2026
